workers.summary: I found four short-horizon ES/NQ edge families that board.md and ledger.csv (N=110) have not covered. Ranked by how testable they are with data we can reach, they are: turn-of-the-month, the overnight-gap reversal (fading the overnight move during the day), FOMC-cycle timing (even weeks and the pre-FOMC drift), and the 5-minute opening-range breakout. Two of them come with published evidence that the edge disappeared after publication or does not survive costs. None is likely to reach the gate's Sharpe ~3 alone, so these are inputs for the hypothesis builder and possible stack parts, not edges. I ran no backtests, so N does not change, and every paper number below comes from search-engine summaries because all primary paper hosts were EGRESS_BLOCKED.

findings.claim: Candidate 1 (most testable): turn-of-the-month (TOTM): long S&P from the close of the last trading day of the month through the 3rd trading day of the next month. McConnell & Xu (FAJ 2008, v64 i2 p49-64): over 1926-2005 investors were on average rewarded for market risk only at turns of the month. Since 1987, the average daily value-weighted excess return in the 4-day window is 0.14%, against -0.01% on the other 16 days. The effect appears in 31 of 35 countries.
findings.evidence: Web search summary of the CFA Institute and IDEAS/RePEc records for McConnell & Xu 2008. Primary PDF not fetched (ideas.repec.org and cfainstitute were not tried or were blocked). Arithmetic from the summary's own numbers: 0.14% x 4 days x 12 months = about 6.7%/yr excess, before costs, invested about 48 days a year. No Sharpe, drawdown or cost figures were found.

findings.claim: The evidence on whether TOTM persisted after publication is mixed. Etula, Rinne, Suominen & Vaittinen, 'Dash for Cash' (RFS 33(1), Jan 2020), report that it persists and attribute it to institutions' month-end liquidity needs. Carcano & Tornero ('Calendar Anomalies in Stock Index Futures') call the TOTM effect in S&P 500 futures the only calendar effect that is significant and persistent. Maberly & Waggoner (Atlanta Fed WP 2000-11) find that TOTM in S&P futures disappears after 1990.
findings.evidence: WebSearch summaries (Aalto news item on the RFS acceptance; etftrends/validea summaries of Etula et al.; Atlanta Fed WP 2000-11 listing). The primary papers were not read.

findings.claim: TOTM can be tested today with data already in the repo, with no new download: data/spx_open_close.csv has S&P daily close from 1990-01-02 to 2026-09-25 (9,251 rows). Close-to-close returns are valid over the whole span, even though index opens before 2010 are not real opens. That leaves 1990-2008 in-sample and 2009-2026 as post-publication out-of-sample, against the Lakonishok-Smidt 1988 and McConnell-Xu 2008 rules.
findings.evidence: Ran head/tail/wc -l on data/spx_open_close.csv: first row 1990-01-02, last row 2026-09-25, 9,252 lines including the header. data/README.md documents the pre-2010 open problem.

findings.claim: Candidate 2 (testable, and the only one that trades daily): the overnight-gap reversal (CO->OC). Fade the close-to-open move during the next open-to-close session. Grant, Wolf & Yu (Journal of Banking & Finance 29(5), 2005, pp. 1311-1327) find highly significant intraday reversals after large opening moves in US index futures over Nov 1987 - Sep 2002. After a bid-ask cost proxy, that significance is sharply reduced. Yu, Rentzler & Wolf (JOIM 3(3), 2005): in NASDAQ-100 futures, last night's return goes mainly with intraday reversals. Della Corte, Kosowski & Wang, 'Market Closure and Short-Term Reversal' (working paper, Nov 2015), report that the CO-OC reversal beats the classic reversal in equity-index, rate, commodity and FX futures. That is cross-sectional, about 100%/day turnover, and no index-futures-only Sharpe was found.
findings.evidence: WebSearch summaries; the IDEAS URL encodes v29 i5 p1311-1327. Every primary host was blocked. This differs from the board's overnight-drift test (long close->open, stack.md) and from H0005 (first half-hour -> last half-hour momentum).

findings.claim: The gap reversal can be tested on two local datasets. (a) data/spx_open_close.csv, 2010-2026: the open is the index's composite first print, a proxy for an ES 09:30 fill (README caveat). (b) FutureSharks S&P minute bars, 2010-2018 (board.md), for a real 09:30 entry and stop. At about 250 possible trades a year it is the only candidate whose frequency could plausibly reach the gate's Sharpe ~3, and the only prior evidence says costs remove most of it.
findings.evidence: board.md 'Data available here'. data/README.md section on spx_open_close.csv: open equals prior close on 6% of days in the 2010s and 0.1% in the 2020s.

findings.claim: Candidate 3a: FOMC-cycle even weeks. Cieslak, Morse & Vissing-Jorgensen (Journal of Finance, Oct 2019): since 1994 the equity premium is earned entirely in weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6 after an FOMC meeting. A long-only even-week strategy returned 11.8% vs 8.3% excess for buy-and-hold over 1994-2015. No independent post-2016 replication was found.
findings.evidence: WebSearch summary (cxoadvisory 'hold stocks only during FOMC even weeks'; Duke scholars record). The paper PDFs on stern.nyu.edu and bis.org were not readable (stern.nyu.edu EGRESS_BLOCKED). No Sharpe, drawdown or cost figure was obtained.

findings.claim: Candidate 3b: the pre-FOMC drift. Lucca & Moench (JF 2015, NY Fed SR512; sample Sep 1994 - Mar 2011): the S&P 500 rose on average 49 bp in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC announcements. Holding only those windows gave an annualized Sharpe above 1.1. Kurov, Wolfe & Gilbert (Finance Research Letters 40, 2021; sample extended to Dec 2019) find the drift essentially disappeared after 2015, with and without press conferences. This is a published case of an edge dying after publication, so the prior is low.
findings.evidence: WebSearch summaries of the VoxEU/CEPR column and the SSRN author page. newyorkfed.org, papers.ssrn.com and skidmore.edu (the Kurov PDF) were EGRESS_BLOCKED. Arithmetic from the summary's own numbers: 49 bp x 8 meetings = about 3.9%/yr gross.

findings.claim: Both FOMC tests are blocked by missing data: no full list of FOMC dates from 1994 to 2026 has been found from here. GitHub raw borisjoffe/FOMC-dates.js (master/dates.csv) returns only 32 dates, 2021-01-27 to 2024-12-18. federalreserve.gov is blocked. The ScrapeFOMC repo only holds a scraper that needs the Fed site. PyPI pyfedwatch 1.2.0 ships no dates.
findings.evidence: Commands: curl raw.githubusercontent.com/borisjoffe/FOMC-dates.js/master/dates.csv -> HTTP 200, 32 rows (main branch: 404). curl federalreserve.gov -> CONNECT tunnel failed, 403. pip download pyfedwatch==1.2.0 and inspected pyfedwatch/fomc.py: dates are a caller argument. curl the ScrapeFOMC master README: 'history (up to 2016)' scraped via selenium from the Fed site.

findings.claim: Candidate 4 (testable, low prior): the 5-minute opening-range breakout (ORB). Zarattini & Aziz, 'Can Day Trading Really Be Profitable?' (SSRN 4416622, 2016-2023; working paper, not peer-reviewed). Rules: trade in the direction of the first 5-minute candle, stop at its other side, target 10R or the close. Reported: 24% hit rate, +0.13R per trade, and 33%/yr on QQQ at 4x leverage. One independent replication on NQ, SPX, Dow, DAX and FTSE CFDs (Jan 2015 - Jun 2026, about 2,900 sessions each) reproduces +0.131R gross on NQ. Net of costs, no market is distinguishable from zero and four of five are negative.
findings.evidence: WebSearch summaries of the SSRN abstract, concretumgroup.com and an mql5.com blog post. mql5.com and papers.ssrn.com are EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the replication's code and cost model were not inspected. It can be tested here only on FutureSharks S&P minute bars, 2010-2018.

findings.claim: Gate implication: candidates 1 and 3 trade only about 8 to 48 days a year and report Sharpe around 1 at best. They cannot reach the gate's annual Sharpe of about 3 alone. At most they could be uncorrelated stack parts (stack.md). Candidate 2 is the only one at about 250 trades a year, and candidate 4 already has external net-of-cost evidence of zero. Every test raises N, so a test is worth spending only where the prior is not already refuted.
findings.evidence: ORG.md gate item 4 (Sharpe ~3). stack.md section 3 (21-day evaluation table). Trade-frequency counts follow from each paper's rules (4 days x 12 months; 8 FOMC meetings a year; even weeks are about half the year).

workers.summary: I pre-registered and tested one new intraday hypothesis: last-half-hour momentum, from Gao, Han, Li & Zhou (2018). The rule takes the sign of the S&P return from the previous 16:00 close to 10:00, enters at the 15:30 open with a percentage stop, and exits at the 15:59 close. All 3 variants lost money net of the 0.6 pt cost: mean R was -0.142, -0.161 and -0.069, and every bootstrap 5th percentile was below -0.09R, so this fails the gate. Before costs the signal was near zero (+0.002 to +0.023R). It was small but positive in 2010-14 and gone in 2015-18, and the 0.6 pt cost is 15-30% of a 4-8 pt stop, so cost and not the signal decides the result.

hypotheses_tested.hypothesis: Last-half-hour intraday momentum (Gao, Han, Li & Zhou 2018): the sign of the return from the previous 16:00 close to 10:00 predicts 15:30-16:00 on the S&P. Variant A: base, 0.20% stop

heads.decision: No candidate edge exists today, and nothing found today should be called one. The only result measured today, last-half-hour momentum (3 variants, run.txt), failed. Net mean R was -0.142, -0.161 and -0.069, every p5 was below zero, and the gross signal was gone in 2015-18. One candidate is worth tomorrow's work: the overnight-gap fade on the S&P (Grant, Wolf & Yu 2005). Five reasons. (1) It trades about daily and stays flat by the close, so it fits prop accounts. TOTM, overnight drift and FOMC weeks all hold overnight, and no worker has checked any firm's overnight-holding rule. (2) The data hunter's SPY 1m file (2019-01-02 to 2025-07-18, 1,645 sessions) gives the first real out-of-sample test this organization has had for an intraday idea, plus NQ 1m 2020-2025 as a second instrument. (3) I checked the dividend adjustment: on 1,003 shared days, adjusted and raw SPY gaps differ by more than 5 bp on only 16 days, all quarterly ex-dividend Fridays, by about 37-46 bp. So the adjusted file matches ES gaps better than raw SPY does. (4) The target is the prior close, so 1R is the gap size (at least 0.15%). That keeps cost a small share of R, which answers the builder's finding that a 0.6 pt cost against a 4-8 pt stop decided the last result. (5) Every sample year is outside the paper's 1987-2002 sample. The prior is weak, because the paper's significance was sharply reduced after costs. The statistical bar is also known in advance: one-sided Bonferroni at N=143 needs z=3.39. On 1,600 trades that is a per-trade Sharpe of 0.085, or about 1.34 a year at 250 trades/yr (computed today). So this is one cheap, fully pre-registered shot, not a favourite. The single best next experiment is this gap fade, count = 1, run exactly as written in /home/user/claude-skills/skills/prop-fleet/agents/daily/2026-10-04/prereg_gapfade_draft.txt. That means one variant: k=1.0 x trailing 20-day gap stdev, entry at the 09:31 open, target at the prior close, 1R stop, exit at 15:59, cost 2 bp round trip. In-sample is SPXUSD 2010-2018, the primary out-of-sample is SPY 2019-2025 and the second out-of-sample is NQ 2020-2025. The decision rule is fixed in advance, and no retuning is allowed if it fails. **שום דבר לא עבר את השער. אין קצה.**
